book: What It Takes to Become a Chess Master
author: Andrew Soltis

steps.title: A real main line
steps.text: This is the Ruy Lopez, one of the oldest and most trusted openings in chess. Both sides developed sensibly and White has castled. Nothing dramatic has happened yet — and that is the point. Before White touches another piece, he already knows what he wants out of the position.

steps.title: The goal, named
steps.text: Here is the difference between a master and a club player. The club player says "I'll attack." The master says something you can actually work toward: rook to e1, pawn to c3, pawn to d4 — a break in the center. Those three arrows are the whole plan. "Attack the king" is a wish. "c3 and d4" is a goal, and every move from now on either serves it or gets rejected.

steps.title: Homework, one move at a time
steps.text:
Now White does the quiet work. Re1 clears the f1 square and adds pressure down the e-file; c3 builds the pawn base that d4 will need. Black sets up the same structure and castles too — but he is copying, not steering.

Notice that none of these moves threaten anything. Each one has a job anyway: they are all rehearsals for the break.

steps.title: Your move — a quiet one

quiz.hint: Black would love to pin your knight with his bishop. One small pawn move makes that impossible.
quiz.praise: h3 is a quiet move with a job. It takes the g4 square away from Black's bishop, so the pin ...Bg4 — the one move that could slow the whole build-up — is simply never available. This is the pattern: before the big break, ask what your opponent wants to do next, and take it away for the price of a pawn move. No threats, no captures. Just one question answered in advance.

steps.text: Black just castled. His next idea is annoying: ...Bg4 would pin your knight to the queen and stall the plan. Find the quiet move that takes that idea off the board before it happens.

steps.title: Black pushes back
steps.text:
Black is not a spectator. Na5 hits your bishop and offers a trade; then c5 strikes at d4 before the pawn even gets there.

This is normal — your opponent has goals too. White's answers keep the plan alive: the bishop steps back but stays aimed at the kingside, and d4 remains on the agenda.

steps.title: The move it was all for

quiz.hint: You have been rehearsing one central pawn push since move eight. Play it.
quiz.praise: d4! The goal, reached. This is why c3 existed, why the rook went to e1, why the bishop retreated to c2 instead of trading on a5. The pattern: quiet moves slowly build a small advantage, and one forcing move collects it. Steering first, cashing in second — never the other way around.

steps.text: Your bishop sits safely on c2, aimed at the king's side. Black's c-pawn has come at you — and it is your move. Time to cash in. Play the break the last ten moves were all about.

steps.title: The center opens
steps.text:
Pawns come off and the position bursts open — on White's terms, at a moment White chose. The rook on e1, the bishop on c2, the knight on f3: every white piece wakes up with a role.

Black's queenside knight is still far from the action. That is what ten moves of steering bought.

steps.title: What you learned
steps.text: Takeaways from this section: 1. Name your goal before you move. "Break with d4" gives every move a test to pass. "Attack" gives you nothing to check a move against. 2. Quiet moves steer; forcing moves cash in. h3 and c3 made no highlights, but they are what made d4 strong. 3. Homework first, break later. Small advantages add up when every move serves the same goal. Next: finding and improving your worst piece — because a goal is only as good as your weakest piece's ability to serve it.
